There are times when I look in the mirror and notice my skin—it looks thin, almost translucent, like it’s not really mine. My husband says I look fine, great even, but how would he know? He doesn’t *feel* it. 

I don't do any special routines or rituals—I just notice. I’ve felt this way for about six months, maybe longer. It’s not constant, but when it comes, it feels absolutely true. I also worry intensely about my skin—lately, I feel like my face is decaying, thinning out, almost translucent, like it’s being eroded by the same toxins. I check the mirror sometimes, but not constantly, and I don’t pick at it or apply special creams repeatedly. I avoid photos, yes, but more because I don’t want to document the decay, not because I’m rearranging my routine around rituals.  

My work is still going fine—I’m designing a new public garden—but I can’t stop thinking that it’s pointless. Why build beauty that’s just going to be poisoned? I function day-to-day, take care of my home, my marriage, but everything feels... temporary. I don’t perform any routines to fix my skin or prevent the catastrophe. I just *know* it’s coming.

Sometimes I check my reflection in the stainless steel just to be sure… but then I see their eyes follow me. I don’t know if I look worse or if they just notice it more. I haven’t missed a day, but I dread the shift. I just wish I knew why they’re so focused on me.  

It’s been going on for months—maybe half a year? I can’t stop thinking about it, but I haven’t told anyone. What if they think I’m imagining it? But how can I be when I *see* it?

I can feel my skin changing—thickening, crawling, like bugs under it. It started on my hands from all the hot water and soap, but now it’s spreading. I know it must be obvious. Doctors on rounds glance at me and look away fast. That’s how I know it’s bad.  

But I still do my job fine. I’m never late, never miss a shift. I don’t pick at my skin or anything like that—just wash my hands often, but isn’t that normal for a dishwasher? I just want people to stop staring. I *know* they see it—that my skin is rotting. It’s not in my head. It’s real.

It’s not just thinking about it—it’s what I *do*. I spend hours every day in the kitchen, between shifts, checking my reflection in spoons or the shiny side of pots. If there’s no surface, I press my fingers along the bridge, measuring, smoothing. I’ll redo my hair constantly, or wear a scarf indoors just to feel less exposed. Even at night, I’ll get up to check the dark window glass. My coworkers joke that I’m obsessed with cleaning, but it’s not the dishes—it’s *me*.  

The thoughts and the checking… they’re tied together. I can’t stop, because if I do, the feeling that everyone’s judging me gets worse. I don’t socialize anymore. It’s exhausting, but I can’t let go of the rituals. They’re the only thing that gives me brief relief.

I just *know* it’s happening—little things like how he texts when he’s away or the way he showers right when he gets home, like he’s washing someone else off. It’s been nearly a year now, and it’s eating at me. I follow him sometimes, check his phone when he’s asleep. But he’s never given me a real reason. I still go to work—I take care of patients at the hospice, and I’m good at my job. I keep my shifts, do my tasks, comfort families. But my mind keeps circling back to this.  

There’s also this thing… I’ve started believing my skin is rotting. Not like a rash or acne—I mean deep down, it’s decaying. I don’t look in the mirror much anymore. I smell it sometimes, I swear. I know people say I look fine, but they don’t feel what I feel. I don’t do any rituals, though—no scrubbing, no changing clothes, no asking for reassurance. I just carry it. It’s all in my head, but it feels so real. The jealousy, the rotting—I can’t shake them. But I’m not crazy in other ways. I know who I am, where I am. I just can’t let go of these thoughts.
D004-D017_h005.question_b:

Because of this, I spend hours every day checking my reflection—in windows, phone screens, any surface that can show me. I’ll tilt my head, change the light, take photos and zoom in, trying to "fix" the angle. I know some of this sounds extreme, but the thoughts won’t stop. If I could just make it look right, maybe I wouldn’t feel so broken. The ritual of checking, fixing, hiding—it’s the only thing that calms the anxiety, even if just for a moment.
